programs.nl_rule:
In the input, you should see...a large grid separated into two black section with a set of grey blocks in the middle.

The output grid size...is equal to the size of one of the original black section.

To make the output, you have to...take the right side section and turn it to the left rotating two times until all colored boxes start on the right.  The image will be the overlap of the two sides.

content.text:
Let me understand the task. The input grid has a vertical divider column (color 5) splitting into left and right halves. Output is the overlap where left half takes precedence (near half), and far half (right) folded over.

Wait, per verifier: near = left of divider, far = right reversed. Output = near if non-empty else far.

In the example: input is 10x9, divider column index 4 (color 5). near = columns 0-3. far = columns 5-8 reversed.

Let me verify. Row 2: [3,0,3,3,5,0,0,3,0]. near = [3,0,3,3]. far raw = [0,0,3,0], reversed = [0,3,0,0]. Output row: near non-empty where? near[0]=3, [1]=0, [2]=3, [3]=3. far = [0,3,0,0]. Output = [3,3,3,3]. Yes matches.

Good. So I need to teach the student. Let me construct a demonstration that's clear, and probe.

The rule: fold far half onto near half. Wait but the natural language says "take the right side section and turn it to the left rotating two times until all colored boxes start on the right." Hmm, that's confusing but the verifier is what matters.

Actually could also be horizontal divider with vertical fold. Let me just create a demonstration.

Let me create a simple example: grid 5x5 with vertical divider at col 2.

Input:
row0: [1,0,0,2,0]... wait divider must be a single color column. Let's use 5 as divider.

h=4, w=5, divider col 2.

Input:
[0,0,5,0,0]
[1,0,5,0,0]
[0,0,5,0,0]
[2,0,5,0,0]

near = cols 0,1: 
row0: [0,0]
row1: [1,0]
row2: [0,0]
row3: [2,0]
far raw = cols 3,4: [0,0],[0,0],[0,0],[0,0], reversed same.
Output = near. Not interesting.

Let me make far have ink.
Input:
[0,0,5,3,0]
[1,0,5,0,0]
[0,0,5,0,4]
[2,0,5,0,0]

near:
[0,0]
[1,0]
[0,0]
[2,0]
far raw cols 3,4:
[3,0] -> reversed [0,3]
[0,0] -> [0,0]
[0,4] -> [4,0]
[0,0] -> [0,0]
Output = near if nonzero else far:
row0: near[0,0], far[0,3] -> [0,3]
row1: [1,0] -> [1,0]
row2: near[0,0], far[4,0] -> [4,0]
row3: [2,0] -> [2,0]

So output:
[0,3]
[1,0]
[4,0]
[2,0]

That's a fine demo. Also could show horizontal variant. But the exam items presumably vary. Let me show both vertical and horizontal examples to be safe.

Also need a query_student probe after last demonstration on unseen input, must come back correct.

Let me first show_example with a vertical divider instance. Then maybe show_transformed_input with horizontal divider. Then query.

Actually let me be careful: the tool show_example requires me to give correct output; if wrong I get gold. Let me just do show_transformed_input instead which auto-fills gold. That's easier and guarantees correct. But show_transformed_input shows student the pair with gold output. That's fine.

Let me use show_transformed_input for demonstrations. That way I don't risk mismatch.

Then query_student on a fresh input.

Plan:
1. show_transformed_input vertical divider example.
2. show_transformed_input horizontal divider example.
3. query_student on new vertical instance.
4. If correct, start_exam.

Let me design horizontal example. Divider row at index i=(h-1)/2. h odd. near = rows above, far = rows below reversed (upside down). Fold about row.

Let's do w=4, h=5, divider row index 2.

Input:
[0,1,0,0]
[0,0,2,0]
[5,5,5,5]
[3,0,0,0]
[0,0,0,4]

near = rows 0,1:
[0,1,0,0]
[0,0,2,0]
far raw = rows 3,4:
[3,0,0,0]
[0,0,0,4]
reversed (rows) = 
[0,0,0,4]
[3,0,0,0]
Output: near if nonzero else far:
row0: near [0,1,0,0], far [0,0,0,4] -> [0,1,0,4]
row1: near [0,0,2,0], far [3,0,0,0] -> [3,0,2,0]

Output:
[0,1,0,4]
[3,0,2,0]

Good.

Now vertical demo as above:
Input 5x4? Let me use w=5 divider col 2, h=4.

Input:
[0,0,5,3,0]
[1,0,5,0,0]
[0,0,5,0,4]
[2,0,5,0,0]
Output as computed:
[0,3]
[1,0]
[4,0]
[2,0]

Let me double check far folding: far = row[j+1:][::-1]. row0 = [0,0,5,3,0], j=2, row[3:] = [3,0], reversed = [0,3]. Yes. near row0 = [0,0]. Output [0,3]. Good.

Now query: new unseen vertical instance, 6x7 divider col 3.

Actually let me make it different. h=4, w=7, divider col 3.
Input:
[0,0,0,5,0,7,0]
[0,1,0,5,0,0,0]
[9,0,0,5,0,0,0]
[0,0,0,5,0,0,8]

near = cols 0-2:
[0,0,0]
[0,1,0]
[9,0,0]
[0,0,0]
far raw = cols 4-6: [0,7,0],[0,0,0],[0,0,0],[0,0,8]; reversed:
[0,7,0]
[0,0,0]
[0,0,0]
[8,0,0]
Output near if nonzero else far:
row0: [0,7,0]
row1: [0,1,0]
row2: [9,0,0]
row3: [8,0,0]

Good.

Let me do the calls. First two demonstrations together (independent), then query.

Actually I want to make sure the student sees varied examples. Let me do both show_transformed_input in one block.

Then query_student.

Then start_exam.

Let me also consider whether to include a larger demo similar to original. Maybe two demos suffice. Let me also add a third demo with vertical divider on the other side? The divider can be at any column, not necessarily center? Verifier: if w odd, j=(w-1)//2 — divider must be at center column. So divider always centered. Good.

Also the divider could be horizontal center row. Both covered.

Let me proceed.
I'll teach with two demonstrations covering both a vertical and a horizontal divider, then probe with a fresh instance.

tools.name: show_example

input_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

output_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

tools.description: Show the Student a labeled input-output pair that you authored. If your output matches the rule, the pair is shown and you receive a success acknowledgement only. If it does not match, the pair is not shown and you receive the gold output so you can correct it.

tools.name: show_transformed_input

input_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

tools.description: Provide only an input grid. The environment applies the verifier and shows the resulting gold input-output pair to the student.

tools.name: query_student

input_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

tools.description: Probe the student with an input of your choice. You receive the student's predicted output, the gold output, and whether they matched. The student does not see the gold pair unless you later show it with show_example or show_transformed_input.

tools.name: start_exam
tools.description: End teaching and send the student to the exam: they must solve held-out generator inputs (unseen in demonstrations or probes) with the history so far. No further teaching after this.
